ch06.title: My Father's Business
ch06.b001: The First Day · A Quieter Temple
ch06.b002: While his parents were on the road to Jericho, Jesus stayed on in the temple through the afternoon, listening to the discussions. The great crowds of Passover week had nearly gone, and he enjoyed the quieter, more decorous atmosphere of the courts. He took no part in the afternoon conferences. When they ended, he walked out to Bethany and arrived just as Simon’s family was sitting down to the evening meal. The three young people were overjoyed to see him, and he stayed the night in Simon’s house. He visited very little that evening. Most of the time he spent alone in the garden, meditating.
ch06.b003: No incident in all his eventful earth career was more humanly thrilling than this first remembered visit to Jerusalem. For the first time in his life he was free to go and come without restraint, free from every sense of responsibility. It was many years before he would know such a period of freedom again, even for a short time.
ch06.b004: The Second Day · Tears on Olivet
ch06.b005: Early the next morning he was up and on his way back to the temple. On the brow of Olivet he paused and wept over the sight before his eyes: a spiritually impoverished people, tradition bound and living under the surveillance of the Roman legions. By early forenoon he was in the temple, his mind made up to take part in the discussions.
ch06.b006: Meanwhile Joseph and Mary had also risen with the dawn to retrace their steps to Jerusalem. They hurried first to the house of their relatives where they had lodged during Passover week, but no one there had seen Jesus. They searched all day and found no trace of him, and at night they returned to their relatives.
ch06.b007: At the second conference Jesus made bold to ask questions, and he took part in the discussions in a very amazing way, though always in a manner consistent with his youth. Sometimes his pointed questions embarrassed the learned teachers of the law, but he showed such candid fairness and such evident hunger for knowledge that most of them were disposed to treat him with every consideration. Then he presumed to question the justice of putting to death a drunken gentile who had wandered outside the court of the gentiles and unwittingly entered the forbidden precincts of the temple. One of the more intolerant teachers grew impatient and, glowering down at him, asked how old he was. Jesus replied, “⟦Q 125:4.3⟧thirteen years lacking a trifle more than four months.⟦/Q⟧” “Then,” rejoined the irate teacher, “⟦Q 125:4.3⟧why are you here, since you are not of age as a son of the law?⟦/Q⟧” When Jesus explained that he had received consecration during the Passover and was a finished student of the Nazareth schools, the teachers with one accord derisively answered, “⟦Q 125:4.3⟧We might have known; he is from Nazareth.⟦/Q⟧” But the leader insisted that the boy was not to blame if the rulers of the synagogue at Nazareth had graduated him at twelve instead of thirteen, and though several of his detractors got up and left, it was ruled that he might continue undisturbed as a pupil of the temple discussions.
ch06.b008: That evening he went again to Bethany, and again he went out into the garden to meditate and pray. It was plain that his mind was occupied with weighty problems.
ch06.b009: The Third Day · The Boy’s Questions
ch06.b010: By the third day the news of this youth from Galilee had spread, and many spectators gathered to enjoy the sight of a boy confusing the wise men of the law. Simon came down from Bethany to see what the lad was up to. All that day Joseph and Mary went on with their anxious search. Several times they even went into the temple, but they never thought to look closely at the discussion groups, though once they came almost within hearing of his voice.
ch06.b011: Before the day ended, the whole attention of the chief discussion group was fixed on the questions Jesus was asking. Among them were these:
ch06.b017: All day long those who listened marveled, and none more than Simon. For more than four hours the boy from Nazareth plied these teachers with thought-provoking and heart-searching questions. He made few comments on what his elders said. He taught by the questions he asked. By the deft phrasing of a question he would at once challenge their teaching and suggest his own. There was in his manner an appealing combination of sagacity and humor that endeared him even to those who resented his youth. He was always eminently fair, and that afternoon he showed the same reluctance to take unfair advantage of an opponent that marked his entire later ministry. He seemed utterly free from any egoistic desire to win an argument for the sake of logical triumph. He was interested supremely in one thing: to proclaim everlasting truth and so effect a fuller revelation of the eternal God.
ch06.b018: When the day was over, Simon and Jesus walked back to Bethany, and for most of the way the man and the boy were silent. Once more Jesus paused on the brow of Olivet, but this time, looking at the city and its temple, he did not weep. He only bowed his head in silent devotion. After supper he again declined to join the merry circle and went out to the garden, where he lingered long into the night. He was trying to think out some definite plan for his lifework, how best he might reveal to his spiritually blinded countrymen a more beautiful concept of the heavenly Father and set them free from their terrible bondage to law, ritual, ceremonial, and musty tradition. But the clear light did not come to the truth-seeking boy.
ch06.b019: The Fourth Day · Beside the Leader
ch06.b020: At breakfast Lazarus’s mother remarked that his parents must be nearly home by now. Jesus did not seem to comprehend that they would be worried about him. He was strangely unmindful of his earthly parents.
ch06.b021: He went again to the temple, this time without pausing on Olivet. The morning’s discussion was given largely to the law and the prophets, and the teachers were astonished at how familiar he was with the Scriptures, in Hebrew as well as in Greek, though they were amazed not so much by his knowledge as by his youth. At the afternoon conference they had hardly begun to answer his question about the purpose of prayer when the leader invited the boy to come forward, sit beside him, and state his own views on prayer and worship.
ch06.b022: The evening before, Joseph and Mary had heard talk of a strange youth who sparred so deftly with the expounders of the law, but it had not occurred to them that he could be their son. They had about decided to go out to the home of Zacharias, thinking Jesus might have gone there to see Elizabeth and John, and thinking Zacharias might be at the temple, they stopped there on their way to the City of Judah. As they walked through the courts, imagine their surprise and amazement when they recognized the voice of the missing boy and saw him seated among the temple teachers.
ch06.b024: Joseph was speechless. But Mary gave vent to her long-pent-up fear and anxiety. Rushing up to the boy, who had risen to greet his astonished parents, she said: “⟦Q 125:6.5⟧My child, why have you treated us like this? It is now more than three days that your father and I have searched for you sorrowing. Whatever possessed you to desert us?⟦/Q⟧” It was a tense moment. All eyes turned to Jesus to hear what he would say. His father looked at him reprovingly but said nothing.
ch06.b025: It should be remembered that Jesus was now supposed to be a young man. He had finished a child’s schooling, had been recognized as a son of the law, and had been consecrated as a citizen of Israel. And yet his mother more than mildly upbraided him before all the people, in the midst of the most serious and sublime effort of his young life, bringing to an inglorious end one of the greatest opportunities ever granted him to act as a teacher of truth and a revealer of the loving character of his Father in heaven.
ch06.b026: But the boy was equal to the occasion. After a moment’s thought he answered his mother: “⟦Q 125:6.7⟧Why is it that you have so long sought me? Would you not expect to find me in my Father’s house since the time has come when I should be about my Father’s business?⟦/Q⟧”
ch06.b027: Everyone was astonished at his manner of speaking. Silently they all withdrew, leaving him standing alone with his parents. Presently the young man relieved the embarrassment of all three when he quietly said: “⟦Q 125:6.8⟧Come, my parents, none has done aught but that which he thought best. Our Father in heaven has ordained these things; let us depart for home.⟦/Q⟧”
ch06.b029: In silence they set out, and they reached Jericho for the night. Only once did they pause, on the brow of Olivet. There the boy raised his staff aloft and, quivering from head to foot under a surge of intense emotion, said: “⟦Q 125:6.9⟧O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, and the people thereof, what slaves you are—subservient to the Roman yoke and victims of your own traditions—but I will return to cleanse yonder temple and deliver my people from this bondage!⟦/Q⟧”
ch06.b030: On the three days’ journey to Nazareth Jesus said little, and his parents said little in his presence. They were truly at a loss to understand their first-born son, but they treasured his sayings in their hearts, even though they could not fully comprehend them. When they reached home, he made a brief statement to them, assuring them of his affection and implying that they need not fear he would again cause them such anxiety. He ended with these words: “⟦Q 125:6.11⟧While I must do the will of my Father in heaven, I will also be obedient to my father on earth. I will await my hour.⟦/Q⟧”
ch06.b031: He kept that promise. Many times in his mind he would refuse to consent to his parents’ well-intentioned but misguided efforts to dictate the course of his thinking or the plan of his work on earth. Yet in every way consistent with his dedication to his Paradise Father’s will, he gracefully conformed to the desires of his earthly father and the usages of his family. Even when he could not consent, he did everything possible to conform. He was an artist in adjusting his dedication to duty to his obligations of family loyalty and social service.
ch06.b032: Joseph was puzzled. But Mary, as she reflected on these experiences, gained comfort. She came to see his words on Olivet as a prophecy of her son’s Messianic mission as Israel’s deliverer. With renewed energy she set to work to mold his thoughts into patriotic and nationalistic channels, enlisting the help of her brother, Jesus’ favorite uncle, and in every other way she addressed herself to preparing her first-born son to lead those who would restore the throne of David and cast off forever the gentile yoke of political bondage.
part2: Part Two: The Hidden Years in Nazareth
ch07.title: A Sudden Parting
ch07.b002: Of all Jesus’ experiences on earth, his fourteenth and fifteenth years were the most crucial. He had begun to be self-conscious of his divinity and destiny, but he had not yet achieved a large measure of communication with his indwelling Adjuster. These two years should be called the great test, the real temptation. No human youth, passing through the early confusions of adolescence, ever experienced a more crucial testing than Jesus did in his transition from childhood to young manhood.
ch07.b003: When he came home from Jerusalem, Mary was happy at first. She thought she had her boy back again, a dutiful son who would now be more responsive to her plans for his future. But she did not bask long in that sunshine. More and more the boy kept company with his father, and less and less did he bring his problems to her. Neither parent could follow his frequent alternation between the affairs of this world and the contemplation of his Father’s business. Frankly, they did not understand him, but they did truly love him. Meanwhile the story of his exploits among the wise men of the temple delighted all Nazareth. For a time his praise was on everyone’s lips; at last, they said, a really great teacher was to come out of Nazareth in Galilee.
ch07.b004: He had become a good yoke maker and worked well with canvas and leather, and he was rapidly becoming an expert carpenter and cabinetmaker. That summer he often climbed the hill to the northwest of Nazareth for prayer and meditation. A little more than a hundred years before, it had been the “high place of Baal”; now it was the site of the tomb of Simeon, a reputed holy man of Israel. From its summit he looked out over Nazareth and the countryside. He would gaze on Megiddo and recall how an Egyptian army had won its first great victory in Asia there, and how later another army had defeated the Judean king Josiah. Not far away lay Taanach, where Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera. In the distance were the hills of Dothan, where Joseph’s brethren had sold him into Egyptian slavery, and farther still Ebal and Gerizim, with their traditions of Abraham, Jacob, and Abimelech. So he turned over in his mind the history of his father Joseph’s people.
ch07.b005: Early that year Joseph set aside the income from his Nazareth and Capernaum property to pay for Jesus’ long course of study in Jerusalem, where he was to go in August of the following year, at fifteen. Yet both parents had begun to have frequent doubts about their first-born son. He was brilliant and lovable, but so hard to fathom, and nothing extraordinary or miraculous ever happened. Scores of times his proud mother had stood in breathless anticipation, expecting to see him do some superhuman thing, and always her hopes were dashed. The devout people of those days believed that men of promise proved their calling by working wonders, and Jesus did none of these things. Still, the family was prospering. Smooth white boards for writing with charcoal multiplied about the house, and Jesus was allowed to resume his music lessons, for he was very fond of playing the harp. Throughout that year it could truly be said that he “⟦Q 126:1.7⟧grew in favor with man and with God.⟦/Q⟧” The prospects of the family seemed good; the future was bright.
ch07.b007: All went well until that fateful Tuesday, September 25. A runner came from Sepphoris with tragic news: Joseph had been severely injured by the falling of a derrick while at work on the governor’s residence. The messenger stopped first at the shop and told Jesus, and together they went to the house to break the news to Mary.
ch07.b008: Jesus wanted to go to his father at once. But Mary would hear of nothing but that she herself must hasten to her husband’s side. She took James, then ten years old, with her to Sepphoris, and directed Jesus to stay home with the younger children until she returned, for she did not know how badly Joseph was hurt. Jesus stayed, and waited.
ch07.b009: Joseph died of his injuries before Mary arrived. They brought him back to Nazareth, and on the following day he was laid to rest with his fathers. There had been no chance to speak to him, no farewell blessing, and that made it seem all the more tragic. Joseph had been an unusual husband and father, and they all missed him.
ch07.b010: Head of the Family at Fourteen
ch07.b011: Just when prospects were good and the future looked bright, an apparently cruel hand struck down the head of the Nazareth household. Every plan for Jesus’ education was demolished. The carpenter boy, just past fourteen, awakened to the realization that he had not only to fulfill his heavenly Father’s commission to reveal the divine nature in the flesh, but that his young human nature must also shoulder the care of his widowed mother and seven brothers and sisters, and another yet to be born. He became the sole support and comfort of the bereaved family: father to his own brothers and sisters, protector of his mother, guardian of his father’s home, the only home he was to know on this world. They were heavy responsibilities, but highly educational and disciplinary ones.
ch07.b012: Jesus cheerfully accepted what had been so suddenly thrust upon him, and he carried it faithfully to the end. One great problem in his life had been tragically solved: he would not now be expected to go to Jerusalem to study under the rabbis. It remained always true that Jesus “sat at no man’s feet.” He was ever willing to learn from the humblest of little children, but he never derived his authority to teach truth from human sources. Even now he knew nothing of Gabriel’s visit to his mother before his birth; he would learn of it only from John, on the day of his baptism.
ch07.b013: As the years passed, the young carpenter increasingly measured every institution of society and every usage of religion by one unvarying test: What does it do for the human soul? does it bring God to man? does it bring man to God? More and more his time and energy went to just two purposes: the care of his family, and preparation to do his Father’s will on earth. That winter it became the custom for neighbors to drop in in the evenings to hear him play the harp, listen to his stories, for he was a master storyteller, and hear him read from the Greek scriptures. There was a fair sum of money on hand at Joseph’s death, and Jesus proved a wise administrator of his father’s estate, liberal but frugal, saving but generous. Yet for all that he and the neighbors could do to bring cheer into the home, Mary and the children remained overcast with sadness.
ch07.b014: A.D. 9 · A Prayer Written on Cedar
ch07.b015: By the middle of his fifteenth year Jesus had a firm grasp on the management of the family. On Wednesday evening, April 17, A.D. 9, Ruth, the baby of the family, was born, and Jesus did his best to take his father’s place in comforting and ministering to his mother through that sad ordeal. For almost a score of years, until he began his public ministry, no father could have loved and nurtured a daughter more affectionately and faithfully than Jesus cared for little Ruth. And he was an equally good father to all the others.
ch07.b016: That year he first formulated the prayer he later taught his apostles, the prayer many know as “The Lord’s Prayer.” After his father’s death he had tried to teach the older children to pray in their own words, as he so enjoyed doing, but they could not grasp his thought and always fell back on their memorized forms. He tried to lead them along with suggestive phrases, and presently, without his intending it, they were all using a prayer built up largely from those very lines. At last he gave up the idea of spontaneous prayers. One evening in October he sat down by the little squat lamp on the low stone table, and on a piece of smooth cedar board about eighteen inches square he wrote out with charcoal the prayer that became from that time the standard family petition.
ch07.b018: That year Jesus was much troubled by confused thinking. Family responsibility had put aside any thought of acting at once on the Jerusalem visitation directing him to “be about his Father’s business.” He rightly reasoned that the care of his earthly father’s family must take precedence over all other duties.
ch07.b019: He had thoroughly considered the Jewish idea of the Messiah and was firmly convinced that he was not to be that Messiah. He longed to help his father’s people, but he never expected to lead Jewish armies against the foreign domination of Palestine, and he knew he would never sit on the throne of David. Nor did he believe that his mission was to the Jewish people alone. But when the time came to go forth as a world teacher, what would he call himself? By what name would those who believed in him know him?
ch07.b020: While turning these things over, he found in the synagogue library at Nazareth, among the apocalyptic books he had been studying, a manuscript called “The Book of Enoch.” He was certain it had not been written by Enoch of old, but it intrigued him, and he read it again and again. One passage especially impressed him, where the term “Son of Man” appeared. The writer described this Son of Man, who before coming to earth to bring salvation had walked through the courts of heavenly glory with the Father of all, and who had turned his back on all that grandeur to come down and proclaim salvation to needy mortals. Jesus understood well that much Eastern mysticism had become mixed into these writings. Yet he recognized that of all the Messianic predictions and theories of a Jewish deliverer, none was so near the truth as this story tucked away in a book only partly accredited. Then and there he decided to adopt “the Son of Man” as his inaugural title. Jesus had an unerring ability to recognize truth, and he never hesitated to embrace it, no matter from what source it came.
ch07.b021: Other questions remained. To what did the prophecies of a national deliverer refer? Was he of the house of David or not? His mother said he was; his father had ruled that he was not, and he had decided he was not. But could his mother, after all, be right? She had often been right before. And what should be his relation to his family, to the Jewish commonwealth, to the Roman Empire, to the gentiles and their religions? He pondered each of these momentous problems while he worked at the carpenter’s bench, laboriously making a living for himself, his mother, and eight other hungry mouths. To his mother, who still held stoutly to the idea of his being the Jewish Messiah, he said nothing of them. He was learning not to speak of all his thoughts. To all appearances he became commonplace and conventional, though he longed for a trustworthy and confidential friend. His problems were too complex for his human associates to comprehend, and the uniqueness of his situation compelled him to bear his burdens alone.
ch07.b023: With his fifteenth birthday Jesus could officially occupy the synagogue pulpit on the Sabbath. On the first Sabbath after it, the chazan arranged for him to conduct the morning service. When all the faithful of Nazareth had assembled, the young man, having chosen his Scriptures, stood up and began to read:
ch07.b027: When he had finished, he sat down, and the people went home pondering the words he had so graciously read to them. Never had his townspeople seen him so magnificently solemn; never had they heard his voice so earnest and sincere, nor seen him so manly, decisive, and authoritative. That afternoon he climbed the Nazareth hill with James, and when they came home he wrote out the Ten Commandments in Greek, in charcoal, on two smooth boards. Martha later colored and decorated them, and for a long time they hung on the wall above James’s small workbench.
ch07.b029: Little by little the family returned to the simple life of earlier years. Clothes and food grew plainer. They had plenty of milk, butter, and cheese, and in season the produce of their garden, but each month called for greater frugality. Breakfasts were very plain; the best food was saved for the evening meal. Mary turned the sale of doves over to James, and with Miriam’s help they bought a second cow and began selling milk to the neighbors. Before the year was out their savings had nearly disappeared, and they faced the need to sell one of the Nazareth houses that Joseph had owned in partnership with his neighbor Jacob.
ch07.b030: The pay of a common carpenter was slowly falling; working early and late, Jesus could earn only about twenty-five cents a day. The tax collector tried to squeeze extra revenue out of him, even threatening to take his harp. Fearing that the Greek scriptures might be confiscated, Jesus presented them on his fifteenth birthday to the Nazareth synagogue library as his maturity offering to the Lord.
ch07.b031: The great shock of that year came at Sepphoris. There was a dispute over the money due Joseph at the time of his death; the treasurer had offered a paltry sum, and Joseph’s brothers had appealed to Herod himself. Jesus stood in the palace and heard Herod decree that his father had nothing due him. After that unjust decision he never again trusted Herod Antipas, and it is not surprising that he once alluded to him as “that fox.” With it went his faint hope of buying a small farm and moving the family out into the country.
ch07.b032: Yet he did not falter, and he was not discouraged. He rented a piece of land just north of the house and divided it into garden plots, and the older children competed keenly over their vegetables. With three cows, four sheep, a flock of chickens, a donkey, a dog, and the doves, they enjoyed much of farm life after all, and even the little ones had their duties. Kept at the home bench, Jesus could no longer mingle with the caravans, so he sent James to the camel lot to gather news of the world. Day by day he did well the present duty. Jesus’ life is the everlasting comfort of all disappointed idealists.
ch07.b033: With the close of his fifteenth year he had passed through that dangerous and difficult time between childhood and the consciousness of approaching manhood. The growth period for mind and body had ended, and now began the real career of the young man of Nazareth.
ch08.title: The Eldest Son Becomes Head of the Family
ch08.b002: When Jesus entered upon his adolescent years, he found himself the head and sole support of a large family. Within a few years of his father’s death all their property was gone, sold piece by piece to keep bread on the table. Yet he was growing ever more conscious of his pre-existence, and he began more fully to realize that he was present on earth, in the flesh, for the express purpose of revealing his Paradise Father to the children of men. No youth on any world has ever had weightier problems to resolve than Jesus faced in those strenuous years from fifteen to twenty. Having tasted adolescence on a world beset by evil and distraught by sin, the Son of Man would become forever the understanding refuge of the perplexed young people of all the worlds of his universe.
ch08.b003: In this sixteenth year he attained his full physical growth. He was a virile and comely youth, increasingly sober and serious, yet kind and sympathetic. His eye was kind but searching; his smile was always engaging and reassuring. His voice was musical but authoritative, his greeting cordial but unaffected. Even in the most commonplace contacts there seemed to be the touch of a twofold nature, the human and the divine, the sympathizing friend and the authoritative teacher in one. Yet it grew harder for his mother and his brothers and sisters to understand him. Mary had given them to understand, as a kind of family secret, that their eldest brother was destined to become the deliverer of the Jewish people; imagine their confusion when Jesus frankly denied all such ideas and intentions.
ch08.b004: That year Simon started to school, and the family was compelled to sell another house. James took charge of teaching his sisters, and later Miriam and Martha took little Ruth in hand. Jewish girls ordinarily received little education, but Jesus maintained, and his mother agreed, that girls should go to school the same as boys; since the synagogue school would not receive them, they conducted a home school especially for them. Jesus himself was closely confined to the workbench. His work was of such superior grade that he was never idle, however slack trade might be. By the end of the year he had about made up his mind that, after rearing his family and seeing them married, he would enter publicly upon his work as a teacher of truth and a revealer of the heavenly Father. He knew he was not to become the expected Jewish Messiah, and he concluded it was next to useless to discuss these matters with his mother. His was such a peculiar mission that no one living on earth could advise him concerning it. Meanwhile he was a real though youthful father to the children, and they truly loved him. Mary grieved to see him toiling at the bench instead of studying with the rabbis at Jerusalem; yet she loved him and deeply appreciated the willing manner in which he shouldered the responsibility of the home.
ch08.b005: A.D. 11, the Wind of the Zealots
ch08.b006: About this time a wind of agitation swept down from Jerusalem and Judea, stirring men to rebel against the payment of taxes to Rome. A strong nationalist party was coming into being, soon to be called the Zealots. Unlike the Pharisees, they were not willing to wait for the Messiah; they proposed to bring things to a head through political revolt. Organizers from Jerusalem made good headway until they reached Nazareth. When they came to see Jesus, he listened carefully and asked many questions, but he refused to join, and his refusal kept many of the young men of Nazareth out of the movement.
ch08.b007: Mary did her best to induce him to enlist, but she could not budge him. She went so far as to hint that his refusal was insubordination, a violation of the pledge he had made on their return from Jerusalem to be subject to his parents. In answer he only laid a kindly hand on her shoulder and, looking into her face, said: “My mother, how could you?” And Mary withdrew her statement. Her brother Simon had already joined the group, and for several years there was something of an estrangement between Jesus and this uncle.
ch08.b008: Trouble now began to brew. About half the Jewish youths of Nazareth joined the nationalists; the other half began to form a group of more moderate patriots, expecting Jesus to lead them. They were amazed when he declined, pleading his heavy family responsibilities. Then a wealthy Jew named Isaac, a moneylender to the gentiles, came forward offering to support Jesus’ family if he would lay down his tools and lead the Nazareth patriots. Jesus, scarcely seventeen, was confronted with one of the most delicate situations of his early life, made doubly hard because the Jewish religion itself was bound up in the agitation against Rome.
ch08.b010: His mother, his uncle, and even his younger brother James all urged him to join the cause. All the better Jews of Nazareth had enlisted, and the young men who held back would enlist the moment Jesus changed his mind. In all Nazareth he had but one wise counselor, his old teacher the chazan, who advised him on his reply to the citizens’ committee when they came to ask his answer to the public appeal. For the first time in his young life Jesus consciously resorted to public strategy. He had always relied on a frank statement of truth, but now he could not declare the full truth; he could not intimate that he was more than a man, nor disclose the mission that awaited his riper manhood. His family was in turmoil, his friends divided, the whole town in a hubbub, and all of it laid at his door, though he had been utterly innocent of any intention to make trouble.
ch08.b011: He stated his position bravely and diplomatically, to the satisfaction of many though not of all. His first duty was to his family. A widowed mother and eight brothers and sisters needed more than money could buy; they were entitled to a father’s watchcare and guidance, and he could not in clear conscience release himself from the obligation a cruel accident had thrust upon him. Loyalty to a dead father forbade his leaving the family, however much money might be offered for their support. It was then that he made his never-to-be-forgotten statement that “money cannot love.” He made several veiled references to his “life mission,” but explained that it, along with everything else, had been given up so that he might faithfully discharge his obligation to his family.
ch08.b012: Everyone knew he was a good father to his family, and his plea won an appreciative response. Some who were not so minded were disarmed by a speech that was not on the program at all. James rose and declared that he was sure Jesus would help to liberate his people if only he, James, were old enough to take charge of the family; and that if they would let Jesus remain “⟦Q 127:2.9⟧with us, to be our father and teacher, then you will have not just one leader from Joseph’s family, but presently you will have five loyal nationalists, for are there not five of us boys to grow up and come forth from our brother-father’s guidance to serve our nation?⟦/Q⟧” That very day the chazan had rehearsed James in his speech, but that was their secret. So the lad brought a tense and threatening situation to a fairly happy ending.
ch08.b013: The crisis passed, but Nazareth never forgot it. Never again was Jesus in universal favor there, and this division, with later happenings, was one of the chief reasons why he would one day move to Capernaum. That year James graduated from school and took over the making of yokes and plows, while Jesus turned more to house finishing and expert cabinet work. Inwardly, too, the year brought great progress. Gradually Jesus had brought his divine and human natures together, by the force of his own decisions and with only the aid of his indwelling Monitor, such as all normal mortals on postbestowal-Son worlds have. So far nothing supernatural had happened in his career except the visit, one night at Jerusalem, of a messenger dispatched by his elder brother Immanuel.
ch08.b015: In his eighteenth year all the family property except the home and garden was disposed of. The proceeds of the last Capernaum property went for taxes, for new tools for James, and for a payment on the old family repair shop near the caravan lot, which Jesus proposed to buy back. With the pressure eased for a while, he took James to the Passover. They set out a day early to be alone and walked by way of Samaria, Jesus pointing out the historic places as his father had once done for him. They talked over their problems, personal, family, and national. James was a very religious lad and looked forward to the day when he could carry the family so that his brother might begin his mission. Jesus did much thinking along the way, particularly at Bethel and at Jacob’s well.
ch08.b016: James noticed the perfunctory and heartless manner of some of the priests, but on the whole he greatly enjoyed Jerusalem. At Bethany, where Simon had now been laid to rest, Jesus presided over the Passover supper as head of the household, having brought the paschal lamb from the temple. The next day James was received into the commonwealth of Israel. That morning, as they paused on the brow of Olivet to view the temple, James exclaimed in wonder while Jesus gazed on Jerusalem in silence, and James could not comprehend his brother’s demeanor. Later James insisted on going back to hear the teachers, secretly hoping to hear Jesus take part as his mother had told. But Jesus asked no questions. It all seemed so puerile and insignificant to this awakening mind of man and God that he could only pity them. To his disappointed brother he made only one reply: “⟦Q 127:3.5⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
ch08.b017: Back in Nazareth Jesus began work in the old repair shop and was greatly cheered to meet so many people each day from all parts of the country, for Jesus truly loved people, just common folks. Several times a year he still read the Sabbath scriptures at the synagogue, ordering the passages so skillfully that one illuminated the other. He never failed, weather permitting, to take the children out on Sabbath afternoons for their nature strolls. He became a prominent member of the young men’s club for philosophic discussion which the chazan now started, and so regained some of the prestige he had lost. In September Elizabeth and John came to visit. The two young men had many talks on very intimate and personal matters, and they agreed not to see each other again until they should meet in their public service, after “the heavenly Father should call” them to their work. John went home content to labor for his mother on their little farm, and never again did they meet until that day by the Jordan.
ch08.b019: On Saturday afternoon, December 3, of that year, death struck the Nazareth family for the second time. Little Amos, the baby brother, died after a week’s illness with a high fever. Through that time of sorrow Mary had her first-born son as her only support, and at last, in the fullest sense, she recognized Jesus as the real head of the family; and he was truly a worthy head. For four years their standard of living had steadily declined, and now the expense of a funeral on top of everything else staggered them. But to his anxious and grieving mother Jesus would only say: “⟦Q 127:3.14⟧Mother-Mary, sorrow will not help us; we are all doing our best, and mother’s smile, perchance, might even inspire us to do better. Day by day we are strengthened for these tasks by our hope of better days ahead.⟦/Q⟧” His sturdy, practical optimism was contagious. All the children lived in an atmosphere of anticipation of better times, and this hopeful courage helped to build strong and noble characters in spite of their poverty. With untiring patience he endured the trials of a difficult mortal existence, living as if he were “seeing Him who is invisible.”
ch08.b020: A.D. 13, a Brother Like a Father
ch08.b021: By his nineteenth year Jesus and Mary were getting along much better. She regarded him less as a son and more as a father to her children. By now he had fully won her to his method of child training, the positive injunction to do good in place of the old method of forbidding evil. At home, and later throughout his public teaching, he always said, “⟦Q 127:4.2⟧You shall do this—you ought to do that.⟦/Q⟧” He exalted the good by commanding it. He had begun wise discipline so early that little punishment was ever needed. The only exception was Jude; on three occasions his punishment was fixed by unanimous decree of the older children and assented to by Jude himself before it was carried out. Jesus never disciplined arbitrarily, and his uniform fairness greatly endeared him to all his family. All the children, particularly the girls, brought him their troubles as they would to an affectionate father.
ch08.b022: James was well-balanced and even-tempered, though less spiritual than Jesus; Joseph was a faithful plodder; Simon a well-meaning dreamer; Jude a firebrand with the highest ideals but an unstable temper. Miriam was level-headed and keenly alive to things noble and spiritual, the belle of the family, if not of the city; Martha was slow but dependable; and baby Ruth, the sunshine of the home, just about worshiped her big brother and father. Jesus had become the unquestioned head of the house. That year Jude started to school, and to meet the expense Jesus had to sell his harp. So disappeared the last of his recreational pleasures. He had loved to play it when tired in mind and weary in body, but he comforted himself with the thought that at least the harp was safe from seizure by the tax collector.
